title: Robustness in Text-Attributed Graph Learning
one_liner: Defend graph models against attacks on both text and structure by adding a detection and recovery layer that catches which nodes are attacked, then fixes predictions accordingly.
lead: A graph is a network of connected points, each labeled with text. Attackers can corrupt either the labels (text) or the connections (structure), and models collapse. This paper shows that no single model is good at defending both attacks at once—there is always a trade-off. The solution: add a detection step that identifies which nodes have been attacked, then use different prediction strategies for attacked versus clean nodes.

problem.h2: Two attacks, one model cannot beat both
paras: A text-attributed graph has nodes connected by edges; each node also carries text (like a document or description). Models use a text encoder to turn text into numbers, then feed those numbers plus the graph structure into a classifier.

Attackers have two levers. They can poison the text (change the document, so the encoder produces wrong numbers). Or they can poison the structure (add or remove edges, breaking the network). A model trained only against text attacks becomes fragile to structure attacks, and vice versa.

The naive approach: train on both attack types at once. It does not work—the model ends up optimizing away from one attack to hide from the other, leaving both partially exposed. There is no single setting that defends both equally well.

callout.b: The catch: models have an inherent trade-off—good at defending text means weak to structure attacks, and vice versa.
callout.html: Add a detection layer that identifies which attack happened, then apply the right defense for that specific attack.

panels.title: 1. The graph under attack
panels.caption: Red nodes: text corrupted. Blue edges: fake connections. Model sees garbage.

panels.title: 2. Single-model trap
panels.viz_args: Defend text? Ignore edges (fails on structure). Defend structure? Ignore text (fails on text).
panels.caption: Every choice breaks something else. Trade-off is unavoidable.

panels.title: 3. Detect which attack happened
panels.caption: Red marks: detected attacked nodes. Ask: is text bad or edges bad?

panels.title: 4. Apply the right fix
panels.viz_args: Text attacked? Use neighbors. Edges attacked? Filter by similarity. Clean? Use all.
panels.caption: Route each node to the defense it needs, not a one-size compromise.

panels.title: 5. Balanced survival
panels.caption: Red and blue both defended. One model, two weapons.

steps.text: On each test node, check if its neighbors look wrong (low similarity) or if its text looks wrong (flagged by a text classifier).

steps.b: Stage 2: Predict with the right strategy
steps.text: Text attacked only? Predict using only neighbor connections, ignoring the bad text. Structure attacked? Filter suspicious neighbors by similarity, use only trusted ones. Clean? Use everything.
Ensemble the three strategies (text-only, structure-filtered, full) weighted by how confident the detection layer is.
Train the text classifier and similarity threshold jointly so detection gets sharper over time.
One model now survives both attacks as well as an oracle that specialized for each—no more trade-off.

object.h2: What the paper changes: the prediction path
paras: Instead of one fixed forward pass from text and structure to label, the paper inserts a detection gate before the final prediction. The gate asks: is this node attacked (and if so, how)? Then it routes the node down a different path. The paths themselves are not new—one uses neighbors only, one filters edges, one uses both. What is new is the router that chooses which path to take.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: attack type per node
hidden.name: Attack type signal (text vs structure vs clean)
paras: The paper measures which kind of attack hit each node. For text attacks, it uses a learned text classifier that outputs 'this node's text is corrupted.' For structure attacks, it checks neighbor similarity: if neighbors are very dissimilar to the node, the edges are probably fake.

This quantity is 'hidden' because the attacker does not label what they did—the defense has to infer it. The paper estimates it by looking at two signals: text quality (from a fine-tuned classifier) and edge quality (how similar the node's text representation is to its neighbors' text representations, measured by cosine similarity—a way of comparing how close two lists of numbers are).

heat.caption: Darker means more confident the attack type detected. Marked nodes are used in the detection example.

reads.html: After seeing how far each neighbor's text embedding sits from the center node's, you can guess if the edges are fake: far away usually means fake. Similarly, if a text classifier trained on clean data outputs 'corrupted', you found a text attack.

The detection uses low-similarity neighbors (cosine similarity below a learned threshold) as a proxy for structure poisoning, and a supervised text detector for text corruption. Both are trained jointly with the main model.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: different attacks need different defenses
paras: A text attack corrupts the encoder's input, so using only the text is dangerous. But the neighbors are still real, so relying on them is safe. Conversely, a structure attack adds fake edges, so trusting all neighbors fails. But the text is real, so the text encoder's output is trustworthy.

The paper's move: detect which attack happened, then swing the model's attention to the side that is clean. For text attacks, ignore text, trust structure. For structure attacks, ignore bad edges, trust text. The router (the detector) is the only new piece—it learns to separate the two cases by looking at similarity and text quality signals during training.

stages.s: Text quality classifier: is this text corrupted?
Edge quality scorer: are these neighbors similar to the node?
Router: which defense should win? (text-only, structure-only, balanced)
Label from the best-matched defense strategy

math.words: weighted ensemble of three predictions: text-only prediction, structure-only prediction, and balanced prediction, weighted by router confidence in each attack type.
math.equation: y = w_text * y_text_only + w_struct * y_struct_only + w_balanced * y_balanced; where w_text, w_struct, w_balanced are router outputs that sum to 1
symbols: prediction using only text and node features, ignoring edges
prediction using only structure and pre-cached text embeddings, ignoring corrupted text
standard prediction using both text and structure
attention weights from the attack detector; learned during training

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the detector outputs: w_text=0.6 (likely text attack), w_struct=0.1, w_balanced=0.3.
Node A's text-only model predicts class 2 with score 0.9.
Node A's struct-only model predicts class 1 with score 0.5.
Node A's balanced model predicts class 1 with score 0.7.
Ensemble: y = 0.6 * 0.9 + 0.1 * 0.5 + 0.3 * 0.7 = 0.54 + 0.05 + 0.21 = 0.80 (class 2 wins, anchored by text-focused route).

If the detector had output equal weights (0.33 each), the ensemble would be 0.33 * 0.9 + 0.33 * 0.5 + 0.33 * 0.7 = 0.70 (still class 2, but less confident), showing how detection confidence shifts the final answer.

math.note: The weights come from the router (the attack detector), not hand-tuned; they learn which defense to trust by seeing which strategy is right on adversarial examples during training.

bars.h2: Defense trade-off and how SFT-auto solves it

charts.title: GNNs with fixed single strategy
charts.note: Defending text well means ignoring structure cues, so structure attacks win. This is the inherent trade-off.

charts.title: SFT-auto (this paper)
charts.note: By routing to the right defense for each attack type, no single attack owns a weakness. All three attack scenarios are handled well.

items.html: If an attacker crafts an attack that looks like the opposite type (structure poison that makes nodes look similar, text poison that mimics good text), the router sends the prediction down the wrong path and both defenses fail. The paper assumes attacks are somewhat independent.
If you filter out too many neighbors by similarity, you throw away real structure. If too loose, you keep fake edges. The paper learns this threshold, but it must be re-tuned for new datasets.

items.b: Text classifier needs labeled corrupted examples
items.html: The detector needs adversarial examples during training to learn what corrupted text looks like. On brand-new attack types, it generalizes poorly.
When the attack types are distinct and detection is accurate, the router ensemble matches an oracle that knows the attack type in advance, achieving single-defense performance on all three scenarios.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small test: take a graph with 100 nodes, 500 edges, and text labels (e.g., paper abstracts on a citation network). Train SFT-auto on clean data. Then create three attack scenarios: (1) corrupt 10 random node texts, (2) add 50 random fake edges, (3) do both. For each attack, measure the accuracy of the full model versus three baselines: a single model trained to survive text attacks, a single model trained to survive structure attacks, and an oracle that knows the attack type. Show that SFT-auto's accuracy sits between the two baseline failures and matches the oracle.
demo.metric_eq: accuracy_sft_auto / (0.5 * accuracy_text_baseline + 0.5 * accuracy_struct_baseline) should be >1.0, proving it beats a simple average of the two single-defense models.
demo.closing: The demo makes concrete: one model can survive as many attacks as two specialists if you teach it to detect the difference.
